content: Tea tree oil is an essential oil extracted from the leaves of the Melaleuca alternifolia tree, which is native to the northeastern coast of New South Wales, Australia. It is distinct from tea oil, which is derived from the seeds of the tea plant (Camellia sinensis or Camellia oleifera) and used as a cooking oil. The name tea tree oil is somewhat misleading, as Melaleuca alternifolia is not a true tea tree (genus Leptospermum) but rather a paperbark tree. The oil itself is clear to pale golden in color and has a fresh, camphor-like odor. It is widely believed to possess cosmetic and medicinal properties, including antiseptic and antifungal effects. Historically, the indigenous Bundjalung people of eastern Australia used tea tree leaves as traditional medicine. They would inhale the oils from crushed leaves to treat respiratory conditions such as coughs and colds. Additionally, they applied crushed leaves to wounds, often followed by a poultice, and prepared infusions from the leaves to address sore throats and skin ailments. The use of the extracted oil became more common after Arthur Penfold published research in the 1920s and 1930s highlighting its antimicrobial activity. His studies demonstrated that tea tree oil was 11 times more effective than phenol in antimicrobial activity. This led to the establishment of a commercial tea tree oil industry, initially relying on natural bush stands of Melaleuca alternifolia. The oil was often distilled on-site using makeshift, wood-fired stills. However, production declined after World War II due to the rise of synthetic antibiotics and reduced interest in natural products. Interest in tea tree oil resurged in the 1970s, leading to the development of commercial plantations and large-scale production of consistent-quality oil. Among the more than 98 compounds in tea tree oil, terpinen-4-ol is primarily responsible for its antimicrobial properties. While Melaleuca alternifolia is the primary source, the oil can also be extracted from Melaleuca dissitiflora and Melaleuca linariifolia. The oil is defined by international standard ISO 4730, which specifies the required levels of 14 components to qualify as tea tree oil. Tea tree oil has been recognized in Australia as a potent antiseptic for many years, even before scientific evidence supported its efficacy. Recent studies have confirmed its role in skin care and the treatment of various conditions. It is a known antifungal agent, effective in vitro against multiple dermatophytes that affect the skin. In vivo studies have shown that shampoos containing 5% tea tree oil are effective in treating dandruff caused by Malassezia furfur, the most common cause of the condition. Tea tree oil is also used in medically formulated cosmetic products and has been suggested to have antiviral properties. Topical preparations of tea tree oil have demonstrated effectiveness against Candida infections in vitro. For moderate acne, a 5% tea tree oil gel has shown comparable efficacy to 5% benzoyl peroxide, though with a slower onset of action. A 2007 study comparing a 5% tea tree oil gel to a placebo found statistically significant results in favor of the tea tree oil. Additionally, tea tree oil is effective in treating insect bites, boils, minor wounds, sunburns, poison ivy, ear infections, and bee stings. Diluted tea tree oil solutions are marketed as remedies for bacterial and fungal infections in pet fish. In pets, tea tree oil can be used to treat skin problems, wounds, insect bites, stings, and ringworm. However, pure tea tree oil applied directly to an animal's skin can sometimes cause irritation, which typically resolves after discontinuation. It is recommended to test the oil on a small area of the animal's skin before broader application. Tea tree oil is also incorporated into toothpastes and mouthwashes, which have been shown to be effective for oral health issues such as bad breath (halitosis), gum disease, and canker sores. Limited research suggests that tea tree oil may have antiviral activity, particularly against the herpes virus, which causes conditions such as cold sores, chickenpox, shingles, and warts. Tea tree oil is primarily used externally, as data on its oral use in humans is limited. Anecdotal reports suggest that oral ingestion of large quantities may cause side effects such as ataxia and drowsiness. A small percentage of individuals may experience allergic reactions to tea tree oil, typically presenting as minor skin irritation. For undiluted tea tree oil, less than 6% of patients observed in studies reported positive skin reactions, while only 1 in 725 patients experienced irritation with a 1% dilution. A case study involving three individuals suggested a possible link between repeated topical use of products containing lavender oil and prepubertal gynecomastia (abnormal breast development in young boys). In one case, the product also contained tea tree oil and other ingredients. The gynecomastia resolved after discontinuing the use of lavender oil-containing products. Cell culture assays indicated that both lavender and tea tree oils exhibit weak estrogenic properties. Researchers noted that other components in these products might have contributed to the gynecomastia, but these components were not tested. Estrogenic activity has also been reported for other essential oils and foods such as almonds and peanuts. Some articles have criticized the methodology of the study, casting doubt on its conclusions. As with many antibiotics, tea tree oil at concentrations of 4% or lower may activate stress responses in bacteria, potentially reducing their sensitivity to antibiotics in vitro. Tea tree oil is not recommended for use in the ears.
